content: The National Blood Service (NBS) is the organization responsible for collecting, testing, processing, and supplying blood and other tissues to hospitals across England and North Wales. In Scotland, these functions are carried out by a separate entity, the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service, which is accountable to the Scottish Executive. The NBS operates as part of the NHS Blood and Transplant, a Special Health Authority within the National Health Service. This authority also includes the Bio Products Laboratory, which provides blood-derived products to hospitals, and UK Transplant, which manages the national organ donor register. The service was originally established in 1946 as the Blood Transfusion Service, a name still commonly used. In 1991, the name was changed to reflect the transition from a regionally based system to a nationally organized one. The NBS currently operates from 15 centers, collecting approximately 2.1 million blood donations annually and supplying around 8,000 units of blood daily. In 2006, service directors proposed a reorganization plan to centralize blood processing and testing into three large supercentres, closing most local laboratories. However, this plan faced opposition from staff and is currently under review, with the future structure of the service yet to be finalized. The NBS relies entirely on voluntary blood donations from the public. Blood donation sessions are held nationwide in various locations, including village halls, mobile collection units (referred to as Bloodmobiles), dedicated blood donation centers in urban areas, and workplaces where companies and organizations host donation events. To be eligible to donate blood, individuals must generally be in good health, weigh at least 50 kg (7 st 12 lb), and be between the ages of 17 and 60. Regular donors in good health may continue donating until the age of 70. Donors are encouraged to give blood up to four times a year. During the donation process, the donor lies on a bed while a sterile needle connected to a collection bag is inserted into their arm. The procedure is not painful and typically takes 5–10 minutes to collect one unit of blood, which is approximately 470–480 milliliters (just under a pint). After donating, donors are offered refreshments, such as tea and biscuits, to help replenish fluids and allow staff to monitor them for any signs of lightheadedness or fainting, which can occur if the donor has not eaten or drunk enough beforehand. It is recommended that donors eat and drink adequately before donating, especially if they are new to the process. The entire donation session usually lasts between 45 minutes and one hour. In addition to whole blood donations, the NBS also collects platelets using specialized machines called cell separators, typically located in city-center blood donation centers. These machines separate platelets from the donor's blood and return the remaining components to the donor. Platelets are essential for blood clotting and are used in the treatment of conditions such as cancer and leukemia. Since platelets have a short shelf life of only five days, maintaining a constant supply is critical. Donors can give platelets every two weeks, with each donation providing 2–3 adult doses. To obtain one adult dose of platelets through whole blood donations, four separate donations would be required. The NBS has faced criticism for its longstanding policy of banning men who have had sex with men (MSM) from donating blood. This policy has sparked protests from university students in both England and Scotland, with some student organizations, such as Birmingham University's Guild of Students, even barring the NBS from setting up recruitment stalls during events like Fresher's Week. Officials within the NBS defend the policy, citing safety concerns. Despite rigorous blood screening processes, no test is 100% accurate, and MSM are statistically at higher risk of carrying bloodborne infections such as HIV. According to 2005 data from the Health Protection Agency, MSM accounted for one-third of newly diagnosed HIV cases in the UK and 46% of all diagnoses since the start of the epidemic in 1981. The NBS also excludes other groups from donating blood, including heterosexual individuals who have engaged in high-risk sexual behaviors, people who have recently undergone acupuncture, tattoos, or piercings, and those who have traveled to countries with high rates of HIV infection.
